entries.title: Thrace
entries.kicker: The roads to the City run through a lost Roman heartland.
paragraphs: Thrace supplied Constantinople with grain, soldiers and the roads joining the capital to the Balkans. Adrianople stood at the meeting of those roads; its rivers and surrounding plains made it a prize for successive emperors and invaders.

Ottoman troops gained a lasting European foothold at Gallipoli in 1354, after an earthquake damaged its defences. Adrianople fell during the 1360s, though its exact conquest date remains disputed. It became the centre from which the Ottoman court directed its European expansion.

The Ottoman victory on the Maritsa in 1371 broke the strength of a major Serbian expedition. By the eve of this siege, Constantinople looks across a countryside increasingly governed, settled and supplied from the Sultan’s side of the frontier.

entries.title: Moesia
entries.kicker: Beyond the Balkan mountains lie the fallen Bulgarian kingdoms.
paragraphs: Moesia is an old Roman name for lands south of the Danube. Medieval Bulgaria raised its own courts and churches here, with Tarnovo a celebrated centre of royal authority, learning and Orthodox devotion.

Ottoman expansion first brought tribute and dependence, then direct conquest. Tarnovo fell in 1393. The defeat of the crusading army at Nicopolis in 1396 was followed by the loss of Vidin, extinguishing the principal surviving Bulgarian royal centres.

The memory of Christian armies has not faded. In 1444 another crusading expedition reached Varna, where King Władysław was killed and Murad II prevailed. The Danube and the mountain passes remain routes by which help—or another army—might come.

entries.title: Macedonia and Thessaly
entries.kicker: Monasteries, mountain passes and the great harbour of Thessalonica.
paragraphs: Thessalonica was the Empire’s great northern harbour, protected by substantial walls and filled with churches, workshops and merchants. Inland, the plains of Thessaly and the passes through Macedonia connected many competing lordships.

Ottoman armies advanced through the region during the later fourteenth century. Thessalonica first surrendered in 1387, returned to Roman rule after the Ottoman collapse at Ankara, and was entrusted to Venice in 1423 when its defenders could no longer sustain it alone.

Murad II took the city on 29 March 1430, ending the Venetian defence. Elsewhere, conquests, tributary arrangements and local resistance overlapped: the countryside did not change hands in a single campaign. Its surviving communities carry memories of several masters.

entries.title: Bithynia
entries.kicker: Across the water stand the cities of the Empire’s former refuge.
paragraphs: Bithynia holds Prusa, Nicaea and Nicomedia, cities tied closely to Constantinople by roads and water. After the Latin capture of the capital in 1204, Nicaea became the seat of an exiled Roman court which eventually recovered Constantinople.

Ottoman expansion pressed against these cities during the early fourteenth century. Prusa fell in 1326 and became an Ottoman capital; Nicaea followed in 1331, and Nicomedia in 1337. Their loss removed the Empire’s principal surviving urban strongholds in this part of Asia.

Prusa’s markets, silk trade and dynastic foundations now sustain a different ruling house. Across the straits, familiar Roman names remain attached to towns whose revenues and roads have long served the Ottoman state.

entries.title: Opsikion
entries.kicker: The southern Marmara shore faces the crossing into Europe.
paragraphs: Opsikion recalls one of the Empire’s old military districts. Here it names the country around the southern Marmara approaches and the lands associated with the Karasi beys, including Balıkesir and Pergamon.

Turkish principalities emerged as Roman control receded in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries. The Ottomans absorbed Karasi in the middle of the fourteenth century, amid disputes within its ruling house; the exact sequence and dating are not entirely secure.

The acquisition brought experienced captains, coastal resources and access towards the Dardanelles. These shores helped turn an Anatolian frontier power towards Europe. A ship, a landing place and a willing local commander could matter as much as a victory inland.

entries.title: Thrakesion
entries.kicker: The western valleys open towards the harbours of the Aegean.
paragraphs: The old Thrakesian lands include fertile western valleys and cities linked to the sea. Turkish rule spread through much of this country around the turn of the fourteenth century, as the houses of Aydın and Saruhan built their own principalities.

Bayezid I annexed western beyliks in 1390, but Timur’s victory at Ankara in 1402 allowed their rulers to return. Ottoman recovery was gradual. Saruhan was absorbed again in the early fifteenth century; the execution of Cüneyd in 1425 ended his long struggle over Aydın.

These coasts have known divided authority. Latin crusaders seized Smyrna’s harbour in 1344, while Turkish rulers held the upper town; Timur overturned that position in 1402. Merchants and sailors have had to reckon with rival powers on the same shoreline.

entries.title: The Cibyrrhaeot Coast
entries.kicker: Harbours and wooded hills recall the Empire’s old naval frontier.
paragraphs: The Cibyrrhaeot name belongs to the Empire’s former maritime military organisation along the southern coast. The southwestern country around Milas, Beçin and the sheltered harbours later became the domain of the Menteşe beys.

The Menteşe principality arose during the later thirteenth century. Bayezid I took its lands around 1390, but the dynasty recovered after Ankara in 1402. Murad II annexed the principality in 1424 and imprisoned its remaining ruling brothers.

The beys left buildings and foundations at Beçin, Milas and Balat. Their maritime ambitions brought them into the same waters as Italian merchants and the Hospitallers of Rhodes. The broken coast offers shelter, timber and many places from which a small flotilla may sail.

entries.title: Phrygia
entries.kicker: Old roads cross a plateau whose rulers also bargained with marriages and wills.
paragraphs: Phrygia’s uplands connect the western valleys with the Anatolian interior. Around Kütahya, the Germiyan dynasty established one of the strongest Turkish principalities of the early fourteenth century, after Roman authority had withdrawn from much of the district.

Parts of Germiyan passed to the Ottomans through a dynastic marriage arrangement in the late fourteenth century. Bayezid I annexed the remaining principality in 1390. Timur restored its ruler after 1402, leaving the territory once more outside direct Ottoman government.

The last ruler, Yakub II, arranged for his lands to pass to Murad II. His death in 1429 completed their incorporation. Kütahya’s charitable foundations and the memory of its court survive a transfer accomplished through inheritance as well as conquest.

entries.title: Anatolikon
entries.kicker: The plateau has carried imperial armies, Seljuk courts and rival Turkish dynasties.
paragraphs: Anatolikon preserves the name of a great Roman military district, rather than a single medieval frontier. Turkish power spread across the interior after the upheavals of the late eleventh century, although Roman campaigns and local strongholds prolonged the struggle.

By the fourteenth century the plateau was divided among Turkish rulers, towns and competing interests. Ottoman authority reached Ankara during that century and expanded farther under Bayezid I. Incorporation came district by district, through pressure, agreements and war.

In 1402 Timur defeated Bayezid near Ankara and took him captive. The Sultan’s state fractured, and several displaced dynasties returned. Ottoman recovery after the civil war made this country part of a reconstructed empire, whose unity is much younger than its ancient roads.

entries.title: Armeniakon
entries.kicker: Rock-cut tombs overlook the valleys of a disputed northeastern country.
paragraphs: The Armeniakon name recalls a Roman military command spread across northeastern Anatolia. Around Amaseia, the river cuts beneath steep cliffs, royal tombs and a fortress: monuments to rulers older than either the Roman emperors or the Turkish sultans.

Turkish dynasties gained power here after the late eleventh century. Ottoman influence reached Amaseia during the late fourteenth century, with its incorporation completed under Bayezid I. After Ankara in 1402, the city became an important refuge and base for his son Mehmed.

Mehmed’s eventual victory in the Ottoman civil war gave this northeastern base a lasting dynastic importance. Farther east, authority remained divided among rival rulers; Trebizond still survives on the coast. The ancient regional name should not suggest that all its historic lands share one master.

entries.title: Paphlagonia
entries.kicker: Forested mountains stand between the inland roads and the Black Sea.
paragraphs: Paphlagonia’s hills, timber and difficult approaches have supported successive local powers. Kastamonu and Sinop became centres of the Candar dynasty, which emerged from the fragmented political world left by weakening Seljuk authority.

Bayezid I took Kastamonu in 1392, while the dynasty retained Sinop. Timur’s victory in 1402 restored Candar power inland. Later struggles divided its lands again: the settlement of 1423 bound İsfendiyar Bey to Ottoman military service and payments from the copper revenues.

İsmail Bey’s independent court still holds Sinop, shown separately on the coast. Inland lordships and Ottoman-controlled approaches form a more complicated patchwork than a single border can convey. Sea trade, mountain roads and dynastic bargains remain closely entangled here.
